1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6.strategy: Prepares ...Nf6 against the e-pawn without letting White push it to e5, and opens the c8-bishop's diagonal. Black builds a solid, flexible set-up and, once the c-pawn is traded for White's d-pawn, plays with a central pawn majority and the half-open c-file. The price is less space and White's lead in development.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6.strategy: Develops a piece at once, controls d4 and e5 and prepares ...Nf6 without allowing e5. Black commits neither the d- nor the e-pawn and keeps the structure flexible. The cost is that White can avoid the open game with a quiet bishop move to b5 that aims at the knight and, after Bxc6, leaves Black with doubled pawns.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e6.strategy: Opens the f8-bishop's diagonal and prepares ...d5, building a compact pawn structure and leaving the knights and the queen to be placed later. The costs are a c8-bishop hemmed in behind the e6-pawn, a weak d6-square and a slower fight for the centre.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nf6.name: Sicilian Defence: Nimzowitsch Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nf6.background: Named after Aron Nimzowitsch, who pioneered it as one of two provocative variations of the Sicilian Defence; it is also known as the Nimzowitsch–Rubinstein Variation. After 3.e5 Nd5 it resembles Alekhine's Defence.
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nf6.strategy: Attacks e4 at once, but White just pushes 3.e5 and the knight must move again, so White gains space and time. Black gets an unusual game built on attacking White's advanced centre, but with best play White keeps the better of it.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 a6.name: Sicilian Defence: O'Kelly Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 a6.background: Named after the Belgian grandmaster Albéric O'Kelly de Galway, who won the Belgian championship thirteen times between 1937 and 1959.
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 a6.strategy: Takes b5 from White's pieces, so that after ...Nf6 and ...e5 White's knight has no jump to that square. The cost is a tempo spent on a pawn move that develops nothing, and White can sidestep the idea with a quiet pawn move.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 g6.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the king's bishop for pressure on the long diagonal. Until the bishop arrives g7 is empty: 3.d4 cxd4 4.Qxd4 attacks the h8-rook at once, so Black must deal with that first.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Qc7.name: Sicilian Defence: Quinteros Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Qc7.background: Sometimes named after the Argentine grandmaster Miguel Quinteros, who introduced the move into first-class play against Henrique Mecking in 1971.
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Qc7.strategy: Controls e5 and keeps Black's set-up flexible, so the game often settles into a standard Sicilian set-up. The cost is an early queen move that develops no piece, and against a quiet plan with c3 and d4 the queen may be badly placed on c7.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 b6.name: Sicilian Defence: Katalymov Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 b6.background: Named after Boris Katalymov, a Soviet and later Kazakhstani player and multiple champion of Kazakhstan. The French grandmaster Christian Bauer favours it and drew Magnus Carlsen with it in 2005.
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 b6.strategy: Prepares ...Bb7 to press on e4 along the long diagonal, but commits Black to a slower plan than the active ...b5, and Black must guard the b5-square against White's pieces. White keeps a slight plus.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Qb6.strategy: Brings the queen out before any minor piece, eyeing b2 and, once ...cxd4 has opened the diagonal, the d4-square. White develops with gain of time against the queen and keeps a lead in development.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Qa5.name: Sicilian Defence: Mongoose Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Qa5.strategy: Pins the d2-pawn against the king, so 3.d4 is illegal for now, but White simply blocks the diagonal and plays d4 next. The queen then does little on a5, and Black is behind in development.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Na6.name: Zukertort Defence: Sicilian Knight Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Na6.strategy: Puts the knight on the rim, where it eyes b4 and c7 but fights for nothing in the centre. White can ignore it and take the centre, or take it with 3.Bxa6 bxa6, which doubles Black's a-pawns.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nh6.strategy: Puts the knight on the rim, where e4 already controls f5, so it has little to do and the centre stays uncontested. White takes the centre at once.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 a5.strategy: Spends a tempo on the a-pawn and gives up b5 for good, since no black pawn can cover that square any more. Once White takes the centre, a white knight or bishop can settle there while Black lags in development.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 h6.name: Sicilian Defence: Bücker Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 h6.strategy: Takes g5 from White's pieces but spends a tempo on a pawn move that does nothing for the centre or development. White takes the centre and enjoys the freer game.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 h5.strategy: Spends a tempo on the rook's pawn and weakens g5 and the kingside, while the centre and development stay untouched. White takes the centre with d4 and develops at leisure.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 f6.strategy: Supports a later ...e5, but takes f6 from the knight, weakens the e8-h5 diagonal and the king, and develops nothing. White takes the centre at once.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d5.strategy: Challenges the centre at once, but White wins a tempo: 3.exd5 Qxd5 4.Nc3 attacks the queen, which must retreat while White follows with d4 and a lead in development.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 e5.strategy: Offers the e-pawn: 3.Nxe5 takes it, and Black can try ...Qe7 to hit the knight and e4, but regains the pawn only at the cost of time and with a lasting weakness on d5.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 b5.name: Sicilian Defence: Polish Gambit
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 b5.strategy: Gives up a pawn: 3.Bxb5 takes it along the open f1-a6 diagonal, and Black's pressure on e4 or on the bishop does not offer enough compensation.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 g5.strategy: Hangs the g-pawn: 3.Nxg5 wins it, since nothing can recapture, with the c8-bishop and the queen both blocked by their own pawns. The weakened kingside offers no compensation.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 f5.name: Sicilian Defence: Brussels Gambit
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 f5.strategy: Offers the f-pawn: 3.exf5 wins it, since the d7-pawn blocks the c8-bishop, and winning it back costs time. The e8-h5 diagonal to Black's king stays open for good.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 c4.strategy: Pushes the c-pawn where it cannot be defended: 3.Bxc4 wins it along the open diagonal and develops the bishop at the same time.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 a6 3.c3.name: Sicilian Defence: O'Kelly Variation, Venice System
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 a6 3.c3.strategy: The main answer: White prepares d4 and a broad pawn centre, as in the usual c3 set-up against the Sicilian, but with the knight already developed for free because ...a6 does little against this plan. Black has to meet the coming centre at once.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 a6 3.c4.name: Sicilian Defence: O'Kelly Variation, Maróczy Bind
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 a6 3.c4.strategy: Uses the spare tempo to clamp down on the centre before the knight reaches c3: the pawns on c4 and e4 together control d5, and c4 also takes b5 away, so Black's ...b5 plan is stopped. A slow, strategic game in which White enjoys more space.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 a6 3.d4.name: Sicilian Defence: O'Kelly Variation, Normal System
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 a6 3.d4.strategy: Opens the centre at once, as in any open game. It is sound, but here ...a6 is a useful extra move for Black: the knight can no longer jump to b5, and Black can strike back in the centre with ...e5 and equalise comfortably.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 a6 3.Nc3.name: Sicilian Defence: O'Kelly Variation, Yerevan System
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 a6 3.Nc3.strategy: Guards e4 and keeps the open game in hand: White can still play d4 next and reach familiar open positions, with ...a6 not necessarily wasted for Black. A flexible, low-risk choice that does not try to punish the move order.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 a6 3.Be2.name: Sicilian Defence: O'Kelly Variation, Aronin System
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 a6 3.Be2.strategy: A modest developing move that prepares castling and keeps the bishop out of reach of ...b5. It neither fights for the centre nor exploits the slow ...a6, so Black is free to expand on the queenside.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 a6 3.b3.name: Sicilian Defence: O'Kelly Variation, Kieseritzky System
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 a6 3.b3.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the queen's bishop on the long diagonal, aiming at the centre and the kingside. Solid but slow: White gives Black time to take space in the centre.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 a6 3.d3.name: Sicilian Defence: O'Kelly Variation, Quiet System
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 a6 3.d3.strategy: A quiet set-up that supports e4 and leaves the other pieces free to choose their squares. It avoids theory, but it gives up the fight for the centre and offers Black an easy game.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 a6 3.g3.name: Sicilian Defence: O'Kelly Variation, Réti System
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 a6 3.g3.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the king's bishop, where it supports e4 and pressures the long diagonal. Sound and flexible, but White spends time on the flank and does not challenge Black's centre.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 a6 3.b4.name: Sicilian Defence: O'Kelly Variation, Wing Gambit
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 a6 3.b4.strategy: A wing gambit that tries to deflect the c-pawn, which guards d4. After 3...cxb4 Black is simply a pawn up and White has no concrete lead in development to show for it.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 a6 3.c3 d5.strategy: The natural central reply: Black challenges e4 at once and denies White the broad pawn centre. White's c3 pawn takes away the c3 square, so a queen recapture on d5 cannot be hit by a knight there.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 a6 3.c3 Nf6.name: Sicilian Defence: O'Kelly Variation, Venice System, Barcza Line
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 a6 3.c3 Nf6.strategy: Attacks e4 at once and forces White to decide whether to advance or defend it. If the pawn advances, Black's knight lands on a central square and Black fights White's space gain by pressure on the pawn chain.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 a6 3.c3 b5.name: Sicilian Defence: O'Kelly Variation, Venice System, Ljubojevic Line
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 a6 3.c3 b5.strategy: Uses the a6 move: Black gains queenside space and prepares a bishop on the long diagonal against e4. The cost is a loosened queenside, where White can aim at the advanced pawns.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 a6 3.c3 d6.name: Sicilian Defence: O'Kelly Variation, Venice System, Steiner Line
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 a6 3.c3 d6.strategy: Concedes the centre to White: the solid pawn on d6 blocks Black's own bishop and does not challenge e4. Black plans a compact fianchetto set-up, but White gets space and the easier game.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 a6 3.c3 d5 4.exd5.strategy: Takes the pawn at once and makes Black justify the central break. Black must recapture or compensate for the pawn, while White aims for a broad pawn centre and keeps a small, lasting edge.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 a6 3.c3 d5 4.d4.strategy: Strikes in the centre at once instead of taking on d5, keeping the pawn tension. Black can take the e4 pawn, and then White has to show enough for it in quick development and open lines.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 a6 3.c3 d5 4.e5.strategy: Gives up the tension for space: the e5 pawn takes d6 and f6 from Black's pieces and cramps the kingside. The pawn needs support and can be attacked at its base, so the game becomes a slow manoeuvring one.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 a6 3.c3 d5 4.exd5 Nf6.name: Sicilian Defence: O'Kelly Variation, Venice System, Gambit Line
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 a6 3.c3 d5 4.exd5 Nf6.strategy: Develops with an attack on d5 instead of recapturing, a pawn offer for quick development and pressure on White's pawns. White can hold the extra pawn, and it is doubtful that Black's play fully pays for it.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 a6 3.c3 d5 4.exd5 Qxd5.strategy: Wins the pawn back at once with the queen. White's c3 pawn takes Nc3, the usual way to chase it, away, so the queen can stand in the centre and Black avoids giving White a two-pawn centre. White is a little ahead in development, but Black has an easy, sound game.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 a6 3.c3 d5 4.exd5 Nc6.strategy: Develops, but overlooks that the pawn on d5 attacks the knight: White simply takes it, and the recapture with the b-pawn leaves Black a clean piece down.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 a6 3.c4 e6.name: Sicilian Defence: O'Kelly Variation, Maróczy Bind, Paulsen Line
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 a6 3.c4 e6.strategy: The usual master choice: Black frees the dark-squared bishop and covers d5 and f5, accepting less space. A compact set-up, from which Black waits for White to commit in the centre.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 a6 3.c4 d6.name: Sicilian Defence: O'Kelly Variation, Maróczy Bind, Robatsch Line
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 a6 3.c4 d6.strategy: A sturdy pawn on d6 holds e5 and prepares a kingside fianchetto, so the bishop works against the d4 square. A playable way to meet the clamp, though the d6 pawn can become a target.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 a6 3.c4 Nc6.strategy: Adds a second attacker to d4, so White's central break is met by a pawn trade and a challenge to the knight. Black gets active piece play and puts pressure on the clamp, at the cost of a lasting hole on d5.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 a6 3.d4 cxd4.strategy: The standard capture: Black trades a wing pawn for White's central one, opens the c-file and ends up with a central pawn majority. The a-pawn has already taken b5 away from White's knight.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 a6 3.d4 e6.strategy: Prepares a compact set-up that covers d5 and f5 and frees the dark-squared bishop, and leaves the recapture on d4 for later. If White trades on c5, the bishop takes back; the move often leads to the same structures as the capture.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 a6 3.d4 d6.strategy: Guards e5 and prepares a normal Sicilian set-up, but lets White swap queens: after dxc5 dxc5 the queens come off with check and Black loses the right to castle. Playable and level, though a poor try for more than equality.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 a6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4.strategy: Recaptures with a centralised knight and heads into open play. Here ...a6 stops the knight from jumping to b5, so White has to find other squares for it and Black has gained a useful move.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 a6 3.d4 cxd4 4.c3.name: Sicilian Defence: O'Kelly Variation, Normal System, Smith-Morra Line
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 a6 3.d4 cxd4 4.c3.strategy: A pawn sacrifice for quick development and open lines: if Black takes, White recaptures with a piece and gets a lead in development with pressure on the c- and d-files. Playable, but Black stands a pawn up if it defends accurately.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 a6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Qxd4.name: Sicilian Defence: O'Kelly Variation, Normal System, Zagorovsky Line
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 a6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Qxd4.strategy: Brings the queen to the centre at once, but ...Nc6 attacks it with a gain of tempo for Black. A slightly eccentric way to recapture that costs time, though the position stays playable.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 a6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Bc4.name: Sicilian Defence: O'Kelly Variation, Normal System, Cortlever Gambit
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 a6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Bc4.strategy: Leaves the d4 pawn alone and develops the bishop toward f7, but White is a pawn down and ...b5 gains time against the bishop. White has no more than the plain recapture offers, and the pawn remains a problem.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 a6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 e5.name: Sicilian Defence: O'Kelly Variation, Normal System, Taimanov Line
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 a6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 e5.strategy: Challenges the knight at once, using ...a6 which takes b5 away, so the knight must retreat to a less useful square. Black gains central space but leaves the d5 square without a pawn guard.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 a6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6.strategy: Attacks the e4 pawn and makes White defend it before choosing a set-up. With ...a6 already played, White's knight has no outpost on b5, so Black can later challenge it with a central pawn thrust. It keeps Black's options open.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 a6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 e6.strategy: A flexible, solid set-up: the pawn takes d5 and f5 from White and frees the dark-squared bishop, while Black decides later where the queen and knights go. White keeps more space, and Black accepts patient defence.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 f5 3.exf5.strategy: Takes the pawn and keeps it: Black's gambit hopes to pull White's e-pawn away from the centre, but White simply gains a pawn. The open diagonals Black has created also weaken the e6 and e5 squares and the king, so White can develop calmly and let Black's compensation fade.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 f5 3.Nc3.strategy: Develops and ignores the gambit offer. If Black takes on e4, White recaptures with the knight and the material is level, but White passes up a free pawn and the chance to exploit the open diagonals against Black's king.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 f5 3.d3.strategy: Defends e4 with a pawn and builds a quiet, solid position. White declines the free pawn: if Black trades on e4, the material is level and Black's king is left with an open diagonal, but White has less than after simply taking.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 f5 3.exf5 Nh6.name: Sicilian Defence: Double-Dutch Gambit
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 f5 3.exf5 Nh6.strategy: Aims to win the pawn back with the knight, which attacks f5 from the edge of the board. It is slow and awkward: the knight does little else there, and White, a pawn up, can simply go on developing while Black's king is still short of cover on the e8-h5 diagonal.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 f5 3.exf5 Nf6.strategy: Develops the knight and covers h5, so queen raids along the e8-h5 diagonal lose their sting. Black is a pawn down and plays for quick development and pressure on f5; a hasty ...d5 stays dangerous, since e6 and e5 are weak squares White can jump to.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 f5 3.exf5 d5.strategy: Takes the centre at once and prepares to win the pawn back with the bishop, but moving the d-pawn leaves e5 and e6 as holes. White checks on b5 and brings a knight to e5, with real threats against the Black king along the e8-h5 diagonal.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.e5.name: Sicilian Defence: Nimzowitsch Variation, Advance Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.e5.strategy: Chases the knight at once and gains space. Black must spend a second move on the same piece, and White's pawn on e5 cramps Black's development, though it also has to be supported against attack in the fight that follows.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nc3.name: Sicilian Defence: Nimzowitsch Variation, Closed Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nc3.strategy: A flexible alternative: it defends e4 against the knight and keeps d4 in reserve, steering for a normal Open Sicilian. White gives up the space-gaining but committal e5 advance, so the game is less sharp and Black has an easy time finding a sound set-up.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.d3.strategy: Defends e4 solidly with a pawn and frees the c1 bishop, but it is a modest move that gives up the fight for space. White has no hurry to challenge the centre, so Black develops freely and equalises without difficulty.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.e5 Nd5.strategy: Puts the knight on the best square available: it is central and nothing attacks it yet, and from there it eyes c3, b4 and f4. Black has lost time, but White's advanced e5 pawn now needs support, and the fight for the centre goes on.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.e5 Ne4.strategy: Moves the attacked knight to the other advanced square, but 4.d3 hits it again with every retreat covered. Black can escape only by checking with ...Qa5+ and trading the knight for a bishop; otherwise it is lost, and the e5 pawn keeps its cramping grip.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.e5 d6.strategy: Ignores the attacked knight: 4.exf6 wins a whole piece, and recapturing leaves Black a knight down for a pawn.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.e5 Nd5 4.Nc3.strategy: Develops with a threat to trade off the centralised knight. White gains another tempo and keeps the extra space, so Black must decide whether to trade or to support the knight.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.e5 Nd5 4.c4.strategy: Kicks the centralised knight at once and gains space, at the price of a weakness on d4 that Black's c-pawn can challenge. The game turns on whether the extra space outweighs the loosened centre; it commits the c-pawn and gives Black targets.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.e5 Nd5 4.Bc4.strategy: Develops with a hit at the centralised knight, but the knight can retreat to b6 and attack the bishop in return. White then has to spend further time on the bishop, so the gain in development is smaller than it looks.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.e5 Nd5 4.Nc3 e6.strategy: Supports the knight with a pawn, so that a trade on d5 can be answered by recapturing with the pawn instead of the queen, and opens the f8 bishop. Black accepts a recapture that leaves a pawn on d5 against White's advanced e5 and fights for the centre from a solid base.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.e5 Nd5 4.Nc3 Nxc3.name: Sicilian Defence: Nimzowitsch Variation, Exchange Variation
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.e5 Nd5 4.Nc3 Nxc3.strategy: Trades the strong knight for White's, and White recaptures with a developing pawn move that opens lines for the queen and the c1 bishop. Black has spent time, while the e5 pawn goes on cramping Black's game. Playable, but the main route is better.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.e5 Nd5 4.Nc3 Nb6.strategy: Retreats the knight that has already moved twice, avoiding the trade and any damage to the pawn structure. Black accepts being cramped by the e5 pawn and lets White build a full centre at leisure.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.e5 Nd5 4.Nc3 e6 5.Nx.strategy: Removes Black's most active piece; Black normally recaptures with the pawn. White keeps the e5 pawn as a cramping spearhead and prepares to strike at the centre at once.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.e5 Nd5 4.Nc3 e6 5.Ne.strategy: Keeps the knight instead of trading it and attacks the loose c5 pawn. Black can defend and keep the strong knight on d5, so White has spent time without dislodging it, though the position stays level.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.e5 Nd5 4.Nc3 e6 5.Bc.strategy: Develops and adds pressure on the knight on d5. Black can trade it off on c3, after which White has quick development but has given up the chance to saddle Black with a pawn on d5 that has to be defended.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.e5 Nd5 4.Nc3 e6 5.Nx.strategy: The natural recapture: Black gets pawns on c5 and d5 against White's e5 and a share of the centre, but those pawns will be under pressure.
Develops a piece but ignores the recapture: White has taken a knight and simply keeps it, a whole piece up.
Attacks the b2 pawn but steps into the knight's reach: 6.Nxb6 takes the queen, and recapturing on b6 wins back only a knight.
Strikes at once at Black's pawn centre: the pawn attacks c5 and backs up e5, so the white centre is firm. White opens the game while Black's pieces are still at home, and play becomes sharp.

Develops and prepares castling, but leaves the centre to Black. The pawn on d5 can advance to gain space while Black's pieces attack e5, and White gives up the chance to open the game while Black's pieces are still at home.

Strikes at the d5 pawn straight away to open lines against Black's centre. It leaves d4 unguarded by a pawn, though, so Black can advance and gain space; the game becomes more closed and White has to watch the e5 pawn.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.e5 Nd5 4.Nc3 e6 5.Nx.name: Sicilian Defence: Nimzowitsch Variation, Main Line
1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.e5 Nd5 4.Nc3 e6 5.Nx.strategy: Develops with pressure on both d4 and e5, so the centre is tested at once while the pawns on c5 and d5 stay in place. The result is a sharp struggle, in which White tends to keep the better chances.
Hits the e5 pawn at once and frees the c8 bishop. But it opens the diagonal to Black's own king, where White's lead in development counts, so Black has to play accurately to hold the balance.

Develops the bishop and prepares castling, but puts no pressure on the white centre. The d5 pawn has no support, and dxc5 opens the d-file against it while White is ahead in development, so Black is under pressure with little to show for it.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nc3 d6.strategy: Stops e4-e5, which would hit the knight again, and prepares to meet d4 by capturing. Black heads for a standard Open Sicilian with the pawn on d6 and a knight on f6, and avoids the cramped games that the e5 advance gives.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nc3 e6.strategy: Opens the f8 bishop and supports the d5 square, so that an advance of White's e-pawn is met by the knight jump to d5 and a pawn recapture in the centre. It keeps the d-pawn free and leads to solid, flexible play.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nc3 Nc6.strategy: Develops a knight to the centre and fights for d4 and e5, keeping every pawn structure open. Black waits to see how White organises and can still head for a normal Open Sicilian, with more choice than a fixed ...d6.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nc3 d6 4.d4.strategy: Opens the centre, trading White's central pawn for Black's c-pawn. White gets space and open lines for the pieces, and the game reaches a main line of the Open Sicilian by a different route.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nc3 d6 4.Bb5+.strategy: Checks to provoke a decision about Black's pieces, hoping to trade the bishop for a knight and ease Black's grip on e4. Black simply develops with a block, so White gets a quiet game without the space the d4 break offers.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nc3 d6 4.g3.strategy: A quiet set-up: the king's bishop is fianchettoed and White delays the central break. It is sound and avoids the heavy theory of the Open Sicilian, but it hands Black time to organise the usual counterplay.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nc3 d6 4.d4 cxd4.strategy: Takes the pawn and trades a wing pawn for a central one, the heart of every Open Sicilian: Black gets a half-open c-file and a healthy central majority, White gets space and a lead in development.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nc3 d6 4.d4 Nxe4.strategy: Grabs the e4 pawn, but 5.Nxe4 wins the knight for it: nothing recaptures on e4, so Black has given a piece for a pawn.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nc3 d6 4.d4 Nc6.strategy: Develops a piece, but 5.d5 drives the knight back at once and gains space for free. Black has not exchanged the d4 pawn, which the whole Sicilian is built around, and White enjoys a clear space advantage.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nc3 d6 4.d4 cxd4 5.N.strategy: Recaptures with the knight, which now dominates the centre. The game is a standard Open Sicilian, where White has more space and Black a sound structure with counterplay on the c-file.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nc3 d6 4.d4 cxd4 5.Q.strategy: Recaptures with the queen, which stands in the centre at once but can be hit by a developing knight and has to move again. White loses time for nothing a knight recapture does not give.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nc3 d6 4.d4 cxd4 5.B.strategy: Checks before recapturing; White can still win back d4, since the pawn is attacked twice and not defended. The check mostly invites a trade of bishop for bishop or knight, which eases Black's game and leaves White's lead in space unused.
